records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access JMIR Mental Health article, 2026
records.decision_reason: The paper validates score-agnostic embedding/clustering and LLM-written cluster descriptions rather than conducting qualitative coding or researcher-led theme construction; it is adjacent evidence on interpretable topic discovery and stability.

Research objective.value: Test whether multilingual speech clustering yields clinically associated groups and whether an LLM can render them interpretable.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Interpretable LLM-based topic modeling described as automating early thematic-analysis stages.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Whisper transcription, Qwen3 embeddings, UMAP and HDBSCAN cluster responses by interview question; Qwen3-14B summarizes up to 30 transcripts per cluster without clinical scores; associations and stability are statistically evaluated and one psychiatrist reads descriptions.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: unsupervised inductive clustering with post-hoc LLM description

Domain.value: depression/suicide-risk spontaneous speech across French, Italian, Chinese, and Spanish cohorts

Number of documents.value: 1,809 French assessments (1,338 people), 116 Italian, 52 Chinese, and 90 Spanish participants/assessment sets

Number of participants.value: 1,596 unique participants across four cohorts, subject to repeated French assessments

Sensitive-data status.value: sensitive mental-health speech; locally processed and de-identified under cohort-specific governance

Exact model/version.value: Whisper large-v3-turbo, Qwen3-Embedding-8B, Qwen3-14B; local open-weight inference

Prompting strategy.value: Qwen3-14B summarizes a random sample of up to 30 cluster transcripts and identifies common content; prompt in Multimedia Appendix 5.
Prompting strategy.anchor: prompt is provided in Multimedia Appendix 5

Human role.value: One board-certified psychiatrist qualitatively reads descriptions; humans do not create/validate source-level codes.

Unit of analysis.value: response transcript to an interview question or grouped-valence questions

Generated outputs.value: HDBSCAN clusters, human-readable LLM descriptions, and clinical/demographic association estimates

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Cluster descriptions derive from disclosed random transcript samples, but source-to-description assertions are not independently audited.

Number of runs or seeds.value: Primary results use a single pipeline run; seed-stability, transcript resampling, repeated description generation, and prompt-wording analyses are reported separately.

Automatic metrics.value: Cramér V, eta-squared, Kruskal–Wallis/chi-square tests, mixed models, stability/overlap measures, and multiple-testing correction

Human-evaluation design.value: Qualitative reading by one psychiatrist, explicitly not clinical validation

Principal results.value: Clusters were associated with clinical scores in three cohorts and descriptions recovered recognizable constructs; effects varied by question/cohort and noise documents were excluded.

Efficiency or cost results.value: Single-GPU processing per interview question took minutes at cloud-equivalent cost under US$1.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Cohort-specific ethics/consent, de-identification, controlled local inference, and no commercial transmission

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report heterogeneous cohorts/measures, small clinical cohorts, one description model, transcription/language differences, demographics/confounding, HDBSCAN noise, and descriptive rather than clinical validation.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: statistically associated clusters and readable labels do not establish qualitative interpretive validity; one psychiatrist and samples of 30 transcripts cannot audit omissions across full clusters.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: qualitative reading rather than a clinical validation

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Adjacent stability/cost benchmark for cluster-first workflows and a reminder to distinguish topic interpretability from coding/theme validity.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access Journal of Medical Internet Research article 28:e85290, 2026
records.decision_reason: The paper develops a human open-coded taxonomy, benchmarks four DeepSeek sizes on dual-human reference annotations over three runs, analyzes recurrent errors, and scales the selected model to full corpora.

Research objective.value: Develop and validate a unified LLM-assisted annotation framework for cross-platform Chinese autism-community analysis.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Human inductive open coding followed by codebook-based LLM topic/identity annotation.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Researchers build/adapt a two-level taxonomy, two humans independently label a reference subset, four DeepSeek configurations classify under fixed prompts at temperature .1 across three runs, and the best model annotates all records after recurrent-error review.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid: inductive taxonomy construction, deductive classification

Domain.anchor: Baidu Tieba, Chunyu Doctor, and Haodf

Public or restricted data.value: publicly accessible posts/consultations; derived datasets restricted by platform terms/privacy

Number of documents.value: 7,535 open-forum posts and 7,687 physician-platform consultations in full analyses

Sensitive-data status.value: public health-community data de-identified; raw consultation text not redistributed

Prompting strategy.value: Fixed Chinese JSON-only prompts with role, label set, definitions, priority/disambiguation rules, and task fields; temperature .1; complete prompts in supplement.

Human role.value: Researchers open-code taxonomy, two coders independently label/adjudicate the benchmark, select the model, and qualitatively classify recurrent errors.

Unit of analysis.value: forum post or consultation record assigned one topic/identity label per task

Generated outputs.value: two-level topic/identity labels, cross-platform distributions, and recurrent-error taxonomy

Baselines.value: two independent human coders and cross-model/scale comparisons

Automatic metrics.value: accuracy, macro F1, Cohen kappa, across-run SD, and downstream group comparisons

Human-evaluation design.value: Double-blind dual annotation with consensus on a reference subset, plus recurrent-error review for errors seen in at least two runs.

Inter-rater reliability.value: averaged human agreement accuracy 81.65%, κ=.767, F1=.758; best model 79.18%, κ=.736, F1=.727 with low SD; task-specific values reported

Principal results.value: Performance improved then plateaued beyond 14B; the 671B model was selected and showed stable near-human agreement, but hundreds of recurrent, semantically patterned errors remained.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Public/de-identified records, platform-policy compliance, alias-only collection, restricted raw data, and formal ethics review deemed unnecessary under stated conditions

Reproducibility resources.value: Complete prompts, code, and settings at GitHub; raw datasets restricted

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report historical/platform drift, Chinese platform/domain scope, one model family, nonexhaustive full-data validation, taxonomy/reference subjectivity, and remaining automated-label error.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: arithmetic averaging across different tasks can obscure weak categories; near-human aggregate agreement does not justify treating the full automated dataset as error-free, especially for systematic recurrent confusions.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Strong benchmark for scale ablation, fixed prompts, repeated runs, human reliability, and recurring-error analysis; less direct for inductive theme generation.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: arXiv preprint submitted 2026-06-14; no peer-reviewed publication identified by 2026-08-24
records.decision_reason: The paper gives a theory-driven qualitative codebook, expert reference set, diagnostic-gated prompt optimization, three-model annotation, multi-level reliability, and public data/code.

Research objective.value: Develop a validated LLM annotation workflow for implicit realism–instrumentalism stance in Bayesian cognitive-science discourse.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Theory-driven interpretive qualitative coding of graded philosophical stance.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Experts create a codebook and label 251 quotations; a diagnostic-aware autoresearch loop optimizes one shared zero-shot prompt on train/development splits; GPT-5.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Pro independently code 6,858 quotations from 210 articles; quote- and article-level reliability is modeled.

Public or restricted data.value: code, corpus data, and expert annotations publicly linked

Number of documents.value: 210 deployment articles; 6,858 extracted quotations; 251 expert-coded reference quotations

Model family.value: OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini

Exact model/version.value: GPT-5.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3 Pro Preview; article-relevance extraction used heavier provider models including GPT-5.2; API snapshots/settings further documented in repository

Prompting strategy.value: One shared zero-shot protocol optimized through accepted prompt mutations, gated by ICC/alpha and anti-shortcut diagnostics such as scale-use distribution.

Human role.value: Experts define the construct/codebook, label reference quotations, set diagnostic acceptance criteria, and interpret corpus-level findings.

Unit of analysis.value: article quotation scored on complementary realism/instrumentalism scales and bands

Generated outputs.value: continuous/banded stance labels and article-level stance estimates
Generated outputs.anchor: continuous scales constrained to sum to 100

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Every label remains linked to an extracted quote/article; public reference annotations and code support audit.

Baselines.value: expert-coded held-out quotations and three independent model providers; earlier candidate prompts as optimization baselines

Number of runs or seeds.value: multi-model independent annotation; candidate prompt experiments; rerun/temperature details in repository, not fully enumerated in the inspected manuscript

Automatic metrics.value: ICC(2,1), Krippendorff alpha, harmonic combined score, distributional diagnostics, article random effects/rank correlations, mixed-effects regression, effect sizes

Human-evaluation design.value: Expert reference coding on 251 quotes with held-out evaluation; details of coder count/expertise and adjudication are reported in methods/repository

Inter-rater reliability.value: held-out prompt ICC=.79, α=.74, combined=.76; deployment ICC=.80, α=.76, combined=.78; article ranks r=.96–.97

Principal results.value: The validated prompt produced substantial model agreement and stable article ranks; most articles mixed stance bands, supporting graded rather than binary coding.
Principal results.anchor: only 1.4% of articles used a single band

Reproducibility resources.value: Public GitHub code, data, codebook, prompt process, and reference annotations

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors frame this as one expert-led domain case; cross-domain validity, provider drift, reference-set size, quotation extraction, and interpretive construct validity remain limited.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: prompt selection optimizes agreement with a small expert reference, so held-out isolation and analyst flexibility must be audited; cross-model convergence can reproduce shared training priors rather than truth.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: qualitative coding has no objective validation score

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Material evaluation baseline for diagnostic-gated prompt search, scale-use anti-shortcut checks, construct-level reliability, and aggregation-aware validation.
Relevance to the proposed ARR project.anchor: per-item agreement can understate or overstate

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access PLOS Mental Health article, published 2026-04-03
records.decision_reason: The study independently performs manual and fully offline open-model thematic analyses of the same caregiver responses, discloses prompts/raw outputs, and compares corresponding and divergent themes.

Research objective.value: Compare manual and privacy-preserving NLP thematic extraction of Japanese caregivers' medical challenges and unmet needs in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Manual thematic analysis and NLP-based thematic extraction.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Two humans independently code and reconcile responses; an offline quantized Cohere Command R+ receives stepwise researcher-perspective/tree-of-thought prompts, generates themes without human editing or access to manual results, and authors map conceptual correspondence afterward.

Domain.value: caregiver-perceived needs in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome in Japan

Public or restricted data.value: restricted free-text health data; requests subject to ethics approval

Number of participants.value: 125 caregivers surveyed; 65 answered the analyzed question

Language.value: Japanese; English translations of prompts/materials supplied

Sensitive-data status.value: potentially identifiable rare-disease free text, locally/offline processed

Model family.value: Cohere Command R Plus open weights

Exact model/version.value: bartowski/c4ai-command-r-plus-08-2024 quantized GGUF variant on two RTX 6000 Ada GPUs

Prompting strategy.value: Stepwise system/user prompts simulating two independent analytic perspectives, comparison, and iterative refinement; full English translations/mock outputs in supplement.

Human role.value: Two humans create the manual analysis and consensus; model themes remain unedited; researchers later compare correspondence and interpret abstractions.

Generated outputs.value: manual categories/subcategories and independent model themes/subcategories with associated response IDs

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Response IDs associated with themes plus translated raw outputs/prompts; authors warn assignment accuracy was not exhaustively verified.

Number of runs or seeds.value: one reported model analysis; prompt/model robustness not tested

Human-evaluation design.value: Two human coders achieve consensus/manual framework; author mapping of manual and model subcategories; no independent blinded model-output evaluator

Inter-rater reliability.value: human simple percent agreement 90%; no formal human-model coefficient

Principal results.value: Most themes corresponded conceptually; one loneliness/information theme was model-only; human analysis supplied more clinical/contextual interpretation, and some model abstractions were not verbatim constructs.
Principal results.anchor: One theme was extracted only by NLP

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: University of Tokyo ethics approval, informed consent, rare-disease privacy restriction, fully offline local inference

Reproducibility resources.value: Full translated prompts, mock/revised prompts, and raw outputs in S1/S2; raw participant data restricted

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report caregiver/self-selection and severity bias, one Japanese rare-disease sample, prompt/model sensitivity, cultural/linguistic bias, possible synthetic/normative abstraction, and unverified response-ID assignments.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: conceptual correspondence was author-judged without blinding or a formal rubric; treating abstract unsupported constructs as synthesis rather than hallucination requires an explicit trace audit.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Strong privacy/open-model case and raw-output companion, but highlights the need for trace-verification, formal mapping, and stability testing.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access Studies in Health Technology and Informatics proceedings chapter, 2026
records.decision_reason: The full chapter reports a multi-stage LLM qualitative-content-analysis pipeline on 28 interviews with deterministic quote linkage and evaluation by five original researchers.

Research objective.value: Evaluate a traceable multi-stage LLM pipeline for supporting qualitative content analysis of interview transcripts.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Qualitative content analysis/modified meaning condensation and thematic structuring.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Transcripts are segmented, progressively coded, aggregated into low- and high-level concepts, and linked to deterministic source quotations; five original researchers inspect the machine hierarchy/quotes against their prior manual work.

Prompting strategy.value: Stage-specific prompts for segmentation, progressive coding, hierarchy construction, concept naming, and deterministic quotation retrieval.

Human role.value: Three researchers established the original analysis (initial interviews jointly, remainder double-coded/consensus); five original researchers evaluate pipeline outputs.

Unit of analysis.value: interview meaning segment linked upward through low- and high-level concepts

Generated outputs.value: 12 high-level and 73 low-level concepts with linked source quotations
Generated outputs.anchor: official full text, Results, 12 HLC/73 LLC

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Full segment-to-code-to-concept hierarchy with deterministic supporting quotations/source links

Human-evaluation design.value: Five original researchers rate/review conceptual hierarchy, clarity, specificity, and quote grounding

Principal results.value: The pipeline generated 12 HLCs/73 LLCs in about 45 minutes with source traceability; experts found broad usefulness but requested more specificity and clearer concept names.

Efficiency or cost results.value: approximately 45 minutes; monetary cost not reported

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report proof-of-concept scale, one corpus/model, dependence on segmentation/prompt design, expert familiarity, and limited evaluation of interpretive depth/stability.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: original analysts are not independent blinded evaluators, and no repeated/model/human-only time comparison is reported; traceability supports audit but does not validate the abstraction hierarchy.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Material provenance baseline: deterministic source quotation linkage and progressive hierarchy, with open questions about plurality and repeated-run stability.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access Journal of Multimorbidity and Comorbidity article, first published 2026-05-28
records.decision_reason: The study runs human and Claude Sonnet 4 analyses in parallel across staged descriptive/interpretive/integrative layers and records convergence, divergence, evidence checks, and revisions.

Research objective.value: Illustrate how LLM analysis can complement human reflexive thematic analysis of multimorbidity/social-care interviews.
Research objective.anchor: primary contribution of this study is methodological

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Braun–Clarke-aligned reflexive thematic analysis with convergence–divergence mapping.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Trained researchers conduct manual exploratory, interpretive, and integrative analysis; Claude Sonnet 4 receives the same prompts in batches of about five interviews; an experienced researcher independently maps themes for convergence, extension, unsupported divergence, or omission and checks evidence/negative cases.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid: human inductive reference plus staged prompt-guided parallel interpretation

Domain.value: multimorbidity, social-care needs, and perceptions of AI-enabled care in England

Sensitive-data status.value: health/social-care interviews, anonymized and processed on a secure institutional workstation

Exact model/version.value: Claude Sonnet 4 via web UI in August 2025; snapshot not reported

Prompting strategy.value: Iteratively refined then fixed prompts for exploratory concerns, implicit emotions/values, and cross-stakeholder integrative comparison; ambiguous outputs rerun.

Human role.value: Humans conduct the reference analysis, design prompts, independently review model outputs, seek negative cases, verify quotes, and make all final thematic decisions.

Unit of analysis.value: whole interview processed in batches of about five; theme comparison at three analytic layers

Generated outputs.value: 12 reference themes plus model convergences, shifts of emphasis, candidate latent themes, and unsupported/overstated interpretations

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Anonymized participant quotes, prompt/output/version records, and subsequent coding-decision logs

Number of runs or seeds.value: ambiguous/unexpected prompts rerun for comparison; systematic run count not reported

Human-evaluation design.value: Experienced qualitative researcher maps conceptual equivalence/divergence against reference themes and analyst triangulation reviews ambiguity/negative cases.

Principal results.value: Claude broadly converged on relational/care themes and introduced candidate framings such as cognitive overload and power asymmetry, but some outputs overstated or conflated evidence and required rejection/reframing.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Original participant consent/ethics, UK GDPR-compliant anonymization, secure institutional workstation, and no identifiable uploads

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report a single model/data context, human-reference dependence, subjective convergence mapping, web-interface opacity, batching, prompt/run variability, and no claim of autonomous validity.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: original themes are treated as a reference but not a gold standard; the same team controls prompt design, mapping, evidence acceptance, and reporting, with no independent blind audit or quantified mapping reliability.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Strong workflow comparator for explicit convergence/divergence ledgers, negative-case search, and retaining unsupported interpretations rather than silently discarding them.

records.decision_reason: This inspected OSF preprint belongs to the same NITA publication family as the fuller peer-reviewed 2026 Qualitative Research in Psychology version of record extracted in research/screening_2025_fulltext_extractions.json as nguyen_trung_nguyen_2026_nita (DOI 10.1080/14780887.2026.2638348). Retain the VOR extraction once and suppress this duplicate evidence/quality row.
records.family_resolution: 2025 SSRN / 2026 OSF / 2026 Qualitative Research in Psychology NITA family; prefer DOI 10.1080/14780887.2026.2638348 and Paper ID nguyen_trung_nguyen_2026_nita from the 2025 companion.

Research objective.value: Develop and demonstrate a narrative-integrated method for AI-supported theme generation without coding.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Narrative-Integrated Thematic Analysis (NITA), a reflexive non-coding thematic-analysis approach.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Two researchers configure a custom GPT-4o, run direct candidate-theme prompts at least three times, reconcile lists, construct/verify individual participant narratives, search for missing themes, compare cases/groups, refine names, and synthesize a meta-narrative under a PERFECT reflexive log.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: inductive theme-first process with iterative application/refinement

Domain.value: community/environmental change and place attachment in Down East, North Carolina

Dataset name.value: Lumivero Environmental Change in Down East sample project

Approximate corpus size.value: about 20,420 words; approximately 2,000 words per interview

Exact model/version.value: GPT-4o through a custom GPT; snapshot/settings not reported

Prompting strategy.value: Recorded conversational prompts for direct theme tables with quotes, quote extension, repeated-list comparison, case narratives, missing-theme search, cross-case comparison, theme naming, and meta-narrative/map generation.

Human role.value: Two researchers familiarize themselves, configure the system, compare runs, verify/extend quotes, accept/reject/subordinate themes, and author the final narrative.

Unit of analysis.value: whole interview/case and cross-case narrative; no segment coding

Generated outputs.value: six-theme framework, case narratives, subthemes, gender cross-case comparisons, meta-narrative, and thematic map
Generated outputs.anchor: framework that consisted of six themes

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Prompt tables request named participant quotations; researchers cross-check narratives/quotes and log prompts/results in a spreadsheet/PERFECT procedure.

Baselines.value: Authors' prior GAITA coding-based analysis of the same dataset

Number of runs or seeds.value: candidate-theme prompt run at least three times; theme-naming prompt twice; no API seeds

Human-evaluation design.value: Two-author reflexive comparison across runs and with prior analysis; source quotes/cases manually checked

Principal results.value: Five of six NITA themes resembled the prior coding-based set; one resistance-to-change theme was new, and initial outputs were topic-like until case/narrative refinement.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Secondary use of public sample data; confidentiality/ethics considered in PERFECT documentation

Reproducibility resources.value: Many prompts/results and complete PERFECT procedure printed in paper/appendix; custom GPT and exact snapshot/raw chats are not archived as a stable package.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors acknowledge one small familiar public dataset, model/prompt dependence, prior-analysis influence, risk of black-box/overreliance, and need for skilled human reflexivity and source checking.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: the first author previously analyzed the same data and the prior theme set is the comparator, so confirmation/dependence is substantial; no independent evaluation or counterfactual coding-free human analysis is provided.

Relationship to prior papers.value: Direct follow-up/dependence family with Nguyen-Trung's 2024 GAITA paper, reusing the same Down East data and research question.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Novel non-coding/case-narrative workflow and stability checkpoint; should be treated as a dependent family rather than independent replication of GAITA.
